imageInfo.caption: Kerbogha directing the siege of Antioch in 1098, in a manuscript illumination of 1337.
imageInfo.creator: Anonymous illuminator
imageInfo.note: A genuine medieval depiction, though made some 240 years after the event and by the other side: Kerbogha is the crowned figure at left, directing crossbowmen against the walls. The armour, the crown and the crossbows are the illuminator's own century, not his. It replaces a locator map of the crusader states, which depicted no person at all. Public domain.

overview: Kerbogha was the atabeg of Mosul who led a coalition army against the crusaders at Antioch in 1098. His defeat allowed the First Crusade to survive one of its greatest crises.
His defeat at Antioch became a turning point in First Crusade narratives, often interpreted by Latin writers as providential rescue.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Kerbogha was the atabeg of Mosul who led a coalition army against the crusaders at Antioch in 1098. His defeat allowed the First Crusade to survive one of its greatest crises.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Kerbogha rose in the Seljuk military world, where commanders and governors competed for authority across northern Mesopotamia and Syria.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Kerbogha, the atabeg of Mosul, is remembered through his dramatic failure to crush the First Crusade at Antioch in 1098, and the sources — mostly crusader — frame him as the embodiment of overconfident Muslim power brought low. They present a proud and powerful commander who assembled a large coalition army to relieve Antioch, only to see the starving, desperate crusaders sally out and rout his force in one of the most improbable victories of the campaign.

The Christian sources, eager to magnify a providential triumph, portrayed him as arrogant and boastful — even staging a scene of his mother warning him against attacking the Franks — so the portrait of haughtiness is partly literary, designed to make his defeat a lesson in pride punished. His failure owed much to the disunity of his coalition, whose emirs did not trust one another.

What the record allows, behind the hostile framing, is a formidable but ultimately unsuccessful commander undone as much by the divisions within his own army as by the crusaders' desperation. He is remembered chiefly as the general who should have destroyed the First Crusade and did not — a figure whose defeat the Christian sources turned into a parable of arrogance.

contentSections.title: As commander at Antioch
paragraphs: After the crusaders captured Antioch, Kerbogha arrived with a large army to besiege them inside the city. Rivalries within his coalition weakened coordination, and the crusaders broke out to defeat him.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Kerbogha died in 1102 after continuing as a regional power in Mosul.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His defeat at Antioch became a turning point in First Crusade narratives, often interpreted by Latin writers as providential rescue.
